day1.title: Tutorial: Deep Learning for Physical Systems
day1.speaker: Raonic Bogdan
day1.abstract: In the first hour of this tutorial, I will give a brief overview of key techniques in physics-based deep learning. I will then dive into state-of-the-art neural operator methods, discussing approaches for both uniform and non-uniform discretizations of physical systems. We will compare the strengths and limitations of different neural approaches and the types of problems they are suited to. The tutorial will cover Fourier and convolutional neural operators for structured data, as well as graph-based neural networks for unstructured domains.

day1.title: Tutorial: Best Practices in Materials Informatics
day1.speaker: Prof. Taylor Sparks
day1.abstract: Materials informatics—the application of data science and machine learning to materials research—has become a powerful approach for accelerating materials discovery and design. Unlike traditional machine learning, materials informatics must contend with small, heterogeneous, and expensive datasets, strong physical constraints, and the need for interpretability and uncertainty awareness. This workshop introduces the foundations of materials informatics, explaining why data-driven methods are needed, how they differ from conventional ML workflows, and how they fit within the structure–property–processing–performance paradigm. The workshop then focuses on best practices for turning materials data into actionable knowledge and ultimately into new materials. Topics include data sourcing and cleaning, featurization and representation of materials, model selection and validation, avoiding common pitfalls such as data leakage, and using uncertainty-aware models for decision-making. Through practical examples and case studies—including predictive modeling and generative approaches—participants will learn how to move from models to real materials applications using open, reproducible tools.

day1.title: Tutorial: An Introduction to Biology via Machine Learning
day1.speaker: Surya Hari
day1.abstract: In this tutorial, we shall cover machine learning and data science concepts related to biology. We will expose the underlying machine learning and biology principles using a few exercises, each covering a different current area in biology. We will use the TRILL package to download, fine tune and save a protein language model like alphafold. We will also build a classification model that uses tabular features to diagnose high grade cancer. Lastly, we will look at differential expression using gaussian mixture models, to identify genes of interest relevant to cancer. Together, we will cover multiple key areas of machine learning research via language models, graph models and classification models and biology via protein language models, gene expression and hallmarks of cancer.

day2.title: Keynote: Big Questions for HPC-AI
day2.speaker: Mr. Addison Snell
day2.abstract: The massive growth of hyperscale AI has pushed the HPC-AI market to a critical inflection point in 2025. The market is increasingly defined by companies spending tens of billions of dollars per year, building massive data centers hundreds of megawatts — even gigawatts — at a time. As a result, national sovereignty sensitivity is on the rise, and we see independent technology tracks from the U.S., China, Japan, the EU, the UK, India, and others. This has significant implications throughout the industry, including for storage, networking, and data management. Addison Snell of Intersect360 Research has been tracking HPC industry dynamics for more than 20 years. In his talk, he will look at the big questions facing the developers, practitioners, and strategy makers in the HPC-AI industry, with research fueled by the HPC-AI Leadership Organization (HALO).

subtimings.title: AI-Enabled Design of Advanced Anti-Corrosion Coating Material
subtimings.speaker: Prof. Yu Yan
subtimings.affiliation: University of Science and Technology Beijing
subtimings.abstract: Corrosion, influenced by environmental factors, poses significant challenges to engineering reliability, with traditional evaluation methods (e.g., outdoor exposure, indoor acceleration) suffering from long cycles, high costs, and poor environmental relevance. Conventional anti-corrosion coatings also face limitations such as passive protection, susceptibility to defects, and environmental issues. To address these, this study focuses on AI-enabled design of advanced anti-corrosion coatings and efficient development of corrosion inhibitors. Key innovations include three AI-driven corrosion inhibitor prediction models: the 3L-DMPNN discriminative model integrating atomic, chemical bond, and molecular features, achieving high generalization for diverse inhibitors; the Inhibitor_Mol_VAE generative model for novel molecule creation; and large language model (LLM)-assisted prediction (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) with optimized prompts and feature selection, yielding IE prediction accuracy up to 89.51%. Additionally, high-throughput experimentation combined with active learning and interpretable machine learning (e.g., AdaBoost, XGBoost, SHAP) was applied for efficient screening of composite corrosion inhibitors, rust converters, and multi-component formulations, identifying optimal ratios (e.g., BTA:Ce(NO₃)₃ = 1:2) and enhancing formulation development efficiency. Multifunctional smart coatings were developed, including corrosion early-warning coatings (via pH/metal ion-induced color/fluorescence changes), self-healing coatings (shape memory, reversible chemical bonds), and multi-performance coatings (anti-aging, antibacterial, anti-icing). These innovations drastically shorten the R&D cycle, reduce costs, and improve corrosion resistance and engineering safety. This research provides a paradigm shift for corrosion protection material development, bridging AI, high-throughput experimentation, and functional material design.

subtimings.title: The LLM revolution in materials research: from data extraction to crystal design
subtimings.speaker: Prof. Taylor Sparks
subtimings.abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 marked a watershed moment for artificial intelligence, one that has rapidly transformed education, knowledge work, and research itself. Materials science is no exception. For over a century, scientists have pursued the prediction and design of crystal structures, progressing from empirical rules to data-driven models. Now, advances in generative AI, including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, and LLMs, are redefining this pursuit. In this talk, I will compare traditional generative frameworks with emerging LLM-based methods for structure generation, highlighting our recent CrysText approach, which uses LLMs for text-conditioned generation of crystallographic information files (CIFs). This strategy achieves precise adherence to specified constraints while accelerating the discovery process. I will also discuss how LLMs are transforming materials data extraction, enabling automated database creation, large-scale literature mining, and data-informed decision-making. Together, these developments signal a new era in which AI is fundamentally reshaping how materials are discovered, understood, and designed.

subtimings.title: AI-Driven Characterisation, Forecasting, and Modelling of Corrosion in Oil and Gas Systems
subtimings.speaker: Dr. Amine Haboub
subtimings.affiliation: Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute (QEERI), HBKU
subtimings.abstract: This presentation highlights QEERI projects at the intersection of AI and corrosion science, developed with local oil and gas partners. We cover three tracks: (1) characterization, using foundation vision models for corrosion classification, fracture-topology dense prediction from microscopy, and corrosion mapping under insulation; (2) forecasting, predicting pipeline wall-thickness and remaining useful life from irregular, high-noise sensor data, and discovery of coupled chemistry correlations; and (3) modelling, applying physics-informed machine learning to stress corrosion cracking, where pit-driven crack initiation motivates meshless, amortized PDE solvers as faster alternatives to traditional numerical simulations.

subtimings.title: GFlowNets: Diverse Generative AI for Molecular and Biological Sequence Design
subtimings.speaker: Prof. Salem Lahlou
subtimings.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI)
subtimings.abstract: Scientific discovery requires exploring vast combinatorial spaces where promising candidates are scattered across multiple regions rather than concentrated at a single optimum. Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) address this by learning to sample objects proportionally to rewards rather than simply maximizing them, enabling diverse high-quality generation. I will present the core ideas behind GFlowNets and demonstrate applications in molecular and biological sequence design, including recent work on mRNA therapeutics that balance competing objectives like stability, translation efficiency, and codon adaptation.

subtimings.title: Design of Programmable Biologics with Discrete Generative Algorithms
subtimings.speaker: Prof. Pranam Chatterjee
subtimings.abstract: The Chatterjee Lab at the University of Pennsylvania develops generative algorithms to design functional biologics directly from sequence. Our work has centered on protein language models that de novo design peptides to bind and modulate undruggable disease targets, with experimental validation across rare neurodegenerative disorders, pediatric cancers, and viral infections. However, because therapeutic design depends not only on binding but also on developability, specificity, and cellular context, we have developed new discrete diffusion modeling algorithms to generate peptides, proteins, mRNAs, and isoform-specific modulators, enable controllable, Pareto-efficient generation. We have extended further to discrete flow-based generative models to refine highly specific, domain- and motif-resolved binders under competing objectives. Beyond therapeutics, we have also applied our discrete generative frameworks to metal-binding peptides and environmental toxins for bioremediation applications. Finally, we’ve recently pioneered a new class of generative models, termed Schrödinger Bridges, that not only model biological states but also the trajectories connecting them, from protein folding to cell-state transitions, establishing a unified and programmable framework for molecular design grounded in physics and context-aware dynamics.

subtimings.title: AI in Biomedicine: Past and Present
subtimings.speaker: Dr. Raghvendra Mall
subtimings.abstract: Dr. Raghvendra Mall is former Director of Computational Biology at the Biotech Research Center of TII in Abu Dhabi, UAE. He is currently Scientific Advisor for Eternal and a senior consultant for QCRI and Mercor. Dr. Mall’s research lies at the intersection of computational biology, immunology, and applied machine learning. His work centers on biological network analysis, including regulatory network inference, master regulator analysis, and disease module identification for therapeutic target discovery. In structural bioinformatics, he develops deep learning and protein language model (PLM)-based approaches for protein property prediction, encompassing protein solubility, crystallization propensity, toxicity, and applications in drug repurposing or novel immunotherapies.

subtimings.title: More than the sum of its parts - studying representations of multi-object naturalistic scenes using computer vision model systems
subtimings.speaker: Surya Hari
subtimings.abstract: Naturalistic scenes are highly complex and we don’t yet have a clear understanding of how the brain relates representations of whole scenes to those of individual objects. Classical theories of vector decomposition, wavelets and sparse coding don’t explain how we understand lion + cage as zoo and lion + tree as wild and threatening. Here, we use vision models as model systems to understand coding principles of complex multi-object visual stimuli. We find universal coding properties common to both human brains and vision models, and that individual units of vision models encode what we call ‘semantic archetypes’ in their receptive fields. With these archetypes as building blocks, multi-object scenes can be represented with combinations of their components’ archetypes or with new archetypes if the semantic interpretation changes. We have hints that archetypes generalize to LLMs and taken together provide a general framework for understanding foundation models as “retrieval engines” that are reminiscent of the index theory of memory, potentially providing new tools for model interpretation and training.

subtimings.title: Data-Efficient Learning for Science via Generative Priors and Meta-Learning
subtimings.speaker: Dr. Ramazan Gokberk Cinbis
subtimings.abstract:
The rapid integration of machine learning into the natural sciences has hit a fundamental data bottleneck. Paradoxically, while modern instrumentation, from genomic sequencers to satellite constellations, generates an abundance of raw data, the high-fidelity labels required for traditional supervised learning remain scarce, expensive, or physically impossible to obtain. In this talk, I will argue that the future of AI4Science involves breakthroughs to move beyond 'big data' dependency toward Data-Efficient Learning. 
I will discuss three key strategies for this transition. First, we explore leveraging generative models and reward-based reinforcement learning to synthesize training signals and adapt foundation models when traditional labels are absent. Second, we address task-space overfitting in meta-learning by focusing on surgical components, such as meta-learning loss functions or low-complexity modules, to achieve rapid model adaptation. Finally, we examine domain-specific language models and the potential of formal reasoning to handle the complexities of bioinformatics and symbolic logic. Ultimately, these advancements aim to transform AI models into robust tools for scientific inference, capable of operating at the frontiers of discovery where labels are often a luxury.

subtimings.title: Bridging the Scientific Data Gap: Generative Synthesis and Robust Generalization
subtimings.speaker: Prof. Alptekin Temizel
subtimings.abstract: While Artificial Intelligence has shown transformative potential across scientific domains, its application in specialized fields like medicine is frequently limited by the quality and nature of scientific data. Unlike general-purpose datasets, scientific data is characterized by scarcity, class imbalance (particularly in rare pathologies), privacy-driven sensitivity, and high structural complexity. This talk will start by addressing the foundational issues of data quality, particularly the challenges of data duplication and inter-observer variability, where experts may provide conflicting labels for the same clinical instance. To mitigate these constraints, we discuss the shift from traditional data processing to AI-driven synthesis, showcasing how Generative Models and Large Language Models (LLMs) can be used for sophisticated data augmentation. However, the ultimate metric of success is not just performance, but generalization. We conclude by examining whether these models are truly generalizable and investigate the alignment gap: whether the features learned by a model align with the biological observations and diagnostic reasoning of medical professionals.

subtimings.title: Recent Advances in Deep Learning in Scientific Computing
subtimings.speaker: Raonic Bordan
subtimings.abstract: This talk will survey recent advances in applying deep learning to scientific computing, spanning operator learning for PDEs, foundation models for physical systems, and generative approaches to uncertainty in chaotic dynamical regimes.

subtimings.title: Enabling Scientific Discovery using Symbolic Regression
subtimings.speaker: Dr. Nour Makke
subtimings.abstract: Machine learning is making its path into natural sciences. A key limitation in ML from a science perspective is the black-box nature of deep neural networks. An alternative is to learn succinct mathematical equations, thus interpretable models, directly from data, allowing for a deeper understanding and scientific reasoning, which facilitates the path toward new scientific discoveries. Symbolic regression is the ML subfield that infers analytical models from data. It has gained growing interest in recent years. Most symbolic regression applications utilize synthetic data. However, recent applications have utilized experimental data measured in high-energy physics and astronomy, showing promise in learning fundamental physical laws and phenomenological models in physics. We present a review of symbolic regression applications to high-energy physics data, highlight the main limitations of symbolic regression, and discuss new perspectives.

speakers.name: Prof. Taylor Sparks
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Dr. Sparks is an Professor of Materials Science and Engineering at the University of Utah. He holds a BS in MSE from the UofU, MS in Materials from UCSB, and PhD in Applied Physics from Harvard University. He was a Royal Society Wolfson Visiting Fellow at the University of Liverpool and a recipient of the NSF CAREER Award and a speaker for TEDxSaltLakeCity. He is active in TMS, MRS, and ACERS societies. He is currently the Editor-in-Chief for the Integrating Materials and Manufacturing Innovation and the Director of Graduate Affairs for the John and Marcia Price College of Engineering. When he’s not in the lab you can find him running his podcast “Materialism,” creating materials educational content for his YouTube channel, or canyoneering with his 4 kids in southern Utah.

speakers.name: Surya Narayanan Hari
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Surya Narayanan Hari is a fourth year PhD student in the biology program at the California Institute of Technology, where he uses AI as model systems to understand the brain. Previously, Surya completed his undergraduate and masters education at Stanford University where he studied Economics, Mathematics and Operations Research. Previously, Surya performed stand up comedy to cancer patients from economically underprivileged backgrounds waiting in line to see a doctor in India, which inspired him to do cancer research at the Dana Farber Cancer Institute between his time at Stanford and Caltech. At Caltech, Surya received the Chen Graduate Innovators award, given to fund radical innovative ideas. Surya is currently on the job market for internships and full time opportunities!

speakers.name: Raonic Bogdan
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Bogdan is a PhD student at ETH Zurich. He holds a Bachelor’s degree in Physics and Mathematics from École Polytechnique and a Master’s in Applied Mathematics from ETH. His research focuses on the intersection of deep learning and scientific computing, including neural operators, foundation models for physics and generative approaches to turbulence modeling.

speakers.name: Prof. Yu Yan
speakers.affiliation: University of Science and Technology Beijing
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Prof. Yu Yan graduated from University of Leeds, UK in 2006 with Ph.D. He was appointed as the Director of UNDP Corrosion and Protection Center in USTB in 2020, which was funded by United Nations in 1985. He also acts as the Editor-in-Chief for journal Anti-corrosion Methods and Materials. He was elected as a Fellow in Institute of Physics, UK for my contribution in corrosion in 2021. His research focuses on corrosion, tribology and materials genome engineering. He has published over 200 SCI indexed papers and 5 books. He is also the PI for 7 NSFC grants.

speakers.name: Dr. Amine Haboub
speakers.affiliation: Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute (QEERI), HBKU
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Dr. Amine Haboub is a Post Doc at the Qatar Environment and Energy Research Institute (QEERI), where he specializes in the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Materials Science. His research focuses on inverse design, physics-informed machine learning, and advanced time-series analysis. His work has appeared in top-tier journals, including the IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence and ICASSP. With over four years of industry experience as a Software Engineer, he bridges theoretical deep learning and practical engineering applications, currently leading projects on AI-driven corrosion prediction and bio-inspired generative design. He holds a PhD in Computer Science and Engineering from Hamad Bin Khalifa University.

speakers.name: Prof. Salem Lahlou
speakers.affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI)
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Salem Lahlou is an Assistant Professor at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI). His research focuses on GFlowNets, LLM reasoning, and uncertainty estimation, aiming to build more capable and reliable AI for science. He is a core contributor to the GFlowNet framework and creator of the torchgfn library. Salem obtained his PhD from Mila and Université de Montréal under Yoshua Bengio, with prior experience at Google Brain, TII, and IBM Research.

speakers.name: Prof. Pranam Chatterjee
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Pranam Chatterjee is an Assistant Professor of Bioengineering and Computer and Information Science and the Africk-Lesley Distinguished Scholar of Innovation at the University of Pennsylvania. His Programmable Biology Group develops new discrete generative models for the de novo design of biologics, spanning from algorithmic theory to pre-clinical validation in vitro and in vivo. The lab specifically develops therapeutics for rare pediatric diseases, infertility, and substance use disorders, as well as molecules for environmental bioremediation. Having earned his SB, SM, and PhD from MIT, Professor Chatterjee has received the MIRA Award, Hartwell Individual Biomedical Research Award, and multiple NIH and foundation grants for his work. He has also co-founded Gameto, Inc., UbiquiTx, Inc., AtomBioworks, Inc., and Recognition Bio, Inc., which translates his research into fertility-related solutions, RNA medicines, and cancer therapeutics, respectively.

speakers.name: Dr. Raghvendra Mall
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Dr. Mall’s career has spanned positions at prestigious institutions such as TII, Caltech, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, QCRI, and KU Leuven. Dr. Mall is a senior IEEE member and was awarded with “Top 30 IEEE Early Career Professional” in 2024. Dr. Mall has made significant contributions to the field with 110+ publications including high-impact journals like Cell, Nature Medicine, Nature, Science Immunology and Nucleic Acids Research with a record of over 5,000 citations. His work has been pivotal in computational immunology, particularly, in understanding the role of PANoptosis in inflammatory diseases, and multi-omics driven analysis of cancer.

speakers.name: Dr. Gokberk Cinbis
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Ramazan Gökberk Cinbiş is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer Engineering at Middle East Technical University (METU). He received his BSc from Bilkent University in 2008, an M.A. from Boston University in 2010, and a PhD from the Université de Grenoble in 2014, following his doctoral research in the LEAR (now THOTH) team at INRIA. His research focuses on data-efficient learning at the intersection of machine learning, computer vision, and natural language modeling. His interests span meta-learning, zero/weakly/few-shot learning, and generative models, with applications to bioinformatics, earth sciences, and robotics.

speakers.name: Prof. Alptekin Temizel
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Alptekin Temizel is a Professor at the Graduate School of Informatics at the Middle East Technical University (METU), Turkey. He earned his Ph.D. from the Center for Vision, Speech and Signal Processing (CVSSP) at the University of Surrey, UK, in 2006. He is the Principal Investigator of the Deep Learning and Computer Vision Research Lab and serves as an NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute Certified Instructor and University Ambassador. From 2016 to 2017, he was on sabbatical at the University of Birmingham, UK. He also collaborates with various companies on the design and deployment of computer vision and AI systems. His research focuses on computer vision, machine learning, deep learning, and GPU computing.

speakers.name: Mr. Addison Snell
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Addison Snell is a veteran of the High Performance Computing industry and the co-founder and CEO of Intersect360 Research, delivering data and insights covering the HPC-AI market and coordinating the HPC-AI Leadership Organization (HALO). Addison is a frequent keynote speaker and panel moderator at industry events, has testified before the U.S.-China Economic & Security Review Commission Congressional Subcommittee, and was named one of 2010’s “People to Watch” by HPCwire. Addison is a competent bridge player, an excellent Scrabble player, and a puzzle and game enthusiast, particularly word puzzles. In 2022 he achieved a life “bucket list” goal of constructing crosswords for the New York Times

speakers.name: Dr. Nour Makke
speakers.title: Professor / Title
speakers.bio: Dr. Nour Makke is a Post Doc at Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI), HBKU and is currently focused on the research and development of interpretable AI solutions for the physical sciences. Her prior experience includes active involvement in high-energy physics experiments conducted at CERN. Dr. Nour completed her PhD at the University of Paris-Sud (now Paris-Saclay) in France.
